subject: parrotfish
title: Every Night This Fish Wraps Itself in a Bubble of Its Own Slime

scenes.text: Every night, this fish wraps itself in a bubble.
It's a parrotfish. At dusk it oozes mucus from glands in its head, until a clear bag covers its body.
That costs about two and a half percent of its daily energy.
The reason crawls out after dark: tiny crustaceans that latch on and drink fish blood.
Scientists stripped the bags off. About 95 percent were bitten. Wrapped fish: only 10 percent.
So that bubble isn't a bed. It's a mosquito net, made of snot.

description:
Some parrotfish, like the bullethead parrotfish of the Great Barrier Reef, wrap themselves in a see-through mucus cocoon every night, secreted from large glands in the head.
Making it costs about 2.5% of the fish's daily energy. In experiments by Alexandra Grutter's team, about 95% of fish whose cocoons were removed were attacked by blood-sucking gnathiid isopods, versus about 10% of cocooned fish.
Would you sleep in a slime bag to avoid mosquitoes?
first_comment: The bags blocked about 9 in 10 blood-sucker attacks. Which animal has the weirdest bedtime routine?
